source.title: Data-Error Scaling Laws in Machine Learning on Combinatorial Mutation-prone Sets: Proteins and Small Molecules
source.authors: Vanni Doffini; O. V. von Lilienfeld; M. Nash

record.file_problem: The full paper and supporting information are present. The text identifies the paper as a preprint under review.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures held-out learning curves for kernel machines on protein and small-molecule mutation-prone datasets, and reports discontinuities, local asymptotic decay, and dependence on shuffling and encoding rather than a single power law. This refines or challenges the power-law form in the tested non-text setting.
record.gate_note: The paper tests learning curves for kernel ridge regression on mutation-prone biological and chemical data, not language-model pretraining, parameter-count scaling, training-compute scaling, or compute-optimal allocation. It reports qualitative curve behavior in figures and describes those results in the text. No numeric MAE values or fitted scaling exponents are stated. Results cited from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: This is not a test of any version. The study measures data-error learning curves of kernel ridge regression, a non-neural, non-parametric method. The data are tiny closed combinatorial spaces (7-residue peptide, 6-atom molecules, 4-site GB1). Under mutant-based shuffling the training data are ordered by mutation count, and the test set is all quintuple mutants, a distribution shift built into the design. The test MAE is not held-out loss of a scaled neural model, and nothing varies in parameters or compute. The departures from a single power law come from this ordering and coverage design, not from scaling neural models in a new modality or regime. V5 names the same power-law form in neural models of other modalities and regimes, so this is a related but different construct. The paper cites Kaplan et al. and contrasts its curves with typical power-law curves, which is why the relation is 'discusses'. Findings are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that KRR learning curves on mutation-prone discrete spaces do not follow a single power law and can be discontinuous. They describe saturated and asymptotic decay regimes conditioned by the mutation orders in the training set. Curves depend on shuffling, encoding, the response function and WT inclusion, and the GB1 experimental data reproduce the mutant-based trends. They add that random shuffling sometimes removes the accelerations, which needs further study, and they frame the implications for designing DMS libraries.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses kernel ridge regression and varies training examples on mutation-prone protein and chemical datasets; it does not use language-model parameter/token/compute scaling or measure compute-optimal allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: Learning-curve behavior changes with shuffling strategy, encoding, response function, mutation-order composition, and WT inclusion. Random shuffling and mutant-based shuffling give different curve shapes.

fits_no_version.finding: With mutant-based shuffling, KRR learning curves show 'saturated' plateaus and sudden drops at mutation-order thresholds, with power-law-like 'asymptotic' decay only within some mutation-order regions. The pattern holds on synthetic peptide, EvoEF, solvation and GB1 data.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In combinatorial mutation spaces, when training data are ordered by mutation count and the test set is higher-order mutants, data-error learning curves are piecewise and discontinuous rather than a single power law.

fits_no_version.finding: Under random or non-hierarchical shuffling, the discontinuities disappear: EvoEF curves show acceleration and deceleration, while chemical and GB1 curves show neither. Encoding switches which decay regime appears. Including the WT sequence mid-curve raises test MAE abruptly.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Learning-curve shape for kernel models on mutational data depends on training-set ordering, encoding and inclusion of the parent sequence.

fits_no_version.finding: Prediction accuracy falls with the mutation count of the test variants and rises with more training data. Predictions form tilted parallel clusters in calibration plots.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Kernel models extrapolate poorly to higher mutation orders, and their prediction errors are clustered and systematic.

record.problems: The reported curve outcomes are mainly qualitative descriptions and figures; no numeric MAE values or fitted power-law exponents are given. The study uses KRR on mutation-prone protein and molecular datasets, so it does not directly establish behavior for language models or compute scaling. The experimental GB1 dataset includes computationally imputed values, and the authors note substantial variability and possible heteroscedastic noise.
record.rows_left_out: No separately reported numeric outcomes were available to add for the additional encoding and shuffling combinations in Figures S2–S7; main-text descriptions were recorded where sufficiently specific. Figures S10–S15 show further calibration-cluster trajectories, but their detailed pointwise results were not separately extracted.

untested.parts: All: no language-model pretraining loss, and no parameter or compute scaling.
Neural models in other modalities or regimes; only kernel ridge regression is studied.
Fitted exponents and compute-optimal splits; no power-law fits are reported.

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked all rows to V5/V7 and labelled V5 'challenges'. That stretches V5, which concerns neural scaling laws in other modalities, to cover classical kernel learning curves under deliberately ordered and distribution-shifted splits. No numbers or fitted exponents are given; results are qualitative descriptions of figures. If curators read V5 to include any data-error learning curve, these rows would at most limit V5's scope for non-i.i.d., mutation-ordered training. They would not challenge it.

versions.untested_parts: Language-model held-out pretraining loss versus parameter count, tokens, or compute.
Fitting power laws on small language-model runs and predicting much larger runs. The paper discusses prediction of higher-order mutants, but does not fit language-model scaling laws.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocation and its growth with compute.
Effects of depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
Image and video models, language models, and the named regimes of repeated data, fine-tuning, and transfer; tested systems are KRR models on mutation-prone protein and small-molecule data.
Downstream language-model task performance as a function of scale or pretraining loss. The study evaluates protein fitness/property prediction, not downstream language tasks.
Fitted exponents and compute-optimal splits; the paper does not estimate these. It tests curve shape and sensitivity to shuffling, encoding, response function, and WT inclusion.

rows.subject: Laplacian kernel machines (kernel ridge regression)

rows.measure: Test mean absolute error (MAE) learning curve
rows.value: Saturated decay in the single-mutant region: error stayed level initially and dropped suddenly near saturation of that mutation order.
rows.note: The reported plateau and sudden drop are not a single power-law curve.
rows.check: KRR learning curve with mutation-ordered training and a distribution-shifted test set; not the scaled neural-model loss V5/V7 name.
